title: Per-group (decoupled) page size for Mamba/attention hybrids — fp8 KV cache yields no capacity gain

title: Hybrid block sizes can invert the hash/block relationship and crash the offload connector
who: vLLM issue #56396, open
quote: Note `block_size (8) < hash_block_size (32)` — the call asks `resolve_block_hashes` to view 32-token-granularity hashes at a *finer* 8-token granularity, but the function only supports the coarsening direction (`block_size >= hash_block_size`, enforced by the divisibility assert). With 8 < 32 the assert `8 % 32 == 0` can never hold, so the crash is deterministic on the first request.
missing: support for a per-group block size smaller than the global `hash_block_size` (the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash layout has "MLA full-attention group @ block_size 32 + SWA/circular-buffer group @ block_size 8"). An open fix PR exists (#56404) but issue #56396 is open.

title: The `min_num_layers` hybrid grouping heuristic is an acknowledged in-tree FIXME

The maintainer pushback recorded on the issue was: "I have an aversion to adding this complexity in order to avoid running a single forward pass for 1 token --- so just want to make sure I understand why the current impl is not working well", and the closer: "Per offline discussion with @xinyu-intel, there is a lot of complexity here. On CUDA/ROCm, we currently do a single extra forward pass, but the passes are 'pure decode' ... On Gaudi plugin, even though there is only one token scheduled, the request is treated as a prefill. Gaudi team will look into improving this." So the question is resolved-as-wontfix-by-design on CUDA/ROCm, and re-opened as an open vendor-specific problem on Gaudi.

title: Bidirectional KV transfer's block-alignment guarantee breaks on stripped thinking traces
who: vLLM NixlConnector Usage Guide "Limitations" section, with a cited open issue #43094
quote: Reasoning models with stripped thinking traces — When using reasoning models (e.g. DeepSeek-R1) that produce thinking traces (`<think>...</think>`), D's KV blocks cover the full token sequence including thinking tokens. If the client strips thinking traces from the conversation history before sending the next turn, the prompt P receives will be missing tokens from the middle of what D generated. The block-alignment logic assumes P's prompt is a prefix of D's sequence, so pulling KV blocks from D in this case transfers cache computed for the wrong token positions, producing incorrect results.

title: NIXL telemetry throughput conflates overlapped transfers and double-counts across TP ranks, so the KV bandwidth bottleneck cannot be measured correctly
who: vLLM issue #33170 (reporter) — closed by the stale bot, never answered by a maintainer
quote: here vLLM calculates the throughput by the `sum of bytes transferred /sum the xfer time`, but if there are multiple transfers overlapped, we can not simply sum each xfer time as the total duration. In real case, the total duration should be shorter if multiple transfers can be in parallel.

A second reporter added: "it treats each rank as independent, so if total bytes_transferred is 1000MB and i have 8 ranks (tp=8), it treats each rank as 125MB and increase count by 8, instead of aggregating 1 transfer of 1000MB". title: vLLM v1 KV cache offloading — the canonical open RFC
who: `orozery` (author), `njhill`, `josephrocca`; open since 2025-06-19 and labelled `RFC`, `keep-open`
quote: Currently, in vLLM v1 there is no in-house solution for offloading KV cache data from the GPU memory to other medium (in particular, CPU memory). The break-even problem is stated by a maintainer in-thread — `njhill`: "Cached CPU blocks would't necessarily have all preceding blocks also in the CPU cache, some prefix might only reside in the GPU cache. For a given cache tier, we may some length threshold below which it's not worth retrieving (and therefore possibly also not worth storing) since it would be faster to recompute." `orozery` concedes the design implication: "I understand this may not be the case, and CPU size could be roughly the same size as the GPU, or larger by a small factor. So you make up a good point."
missing: an eviction-time (not compute-time) GPU→CPU save hook, and a decision on the GPU-block "next-in-line" notification — "since we want this to be async, this will require changes to vllm's core, allowing the connector to be notified on 'soon-to-be-evicted' GPU blocks." The thread ends without resolution.

title: SGLang HiCache load-back does not overlap the forward pass at all
who: `qidaye`, filed 2026-09-08, still open
quote: The consequence is that the layer-wise pipeline (`LayerDoneCounter` / `wait_until` in the attention layers) almost never overlaps anything: by the time `start_loading` returns and the batch is built and launched, every copy has already landed. … "So the scheduler thread stalls for the full enqueue duration, and the forward that should have hidden the H2D copies only starts once they are essentially complete." Measured table in the body: per-layer `load_to_device_per_layer` submission (CPU) `~2.4 ms`; `start_loading` per burst (78 layers x 2 pools) `~375 ms`; **"share of the H2D copy time that overlapped compute | 0.04 %"**.
missing: the proposed fix (move the burst to a FIFO daemon thread behind `SGLANG_HICACHE_ASYNC_LOAD_ENQUEUE`, default off) is unimplemented, and the correctness work it requires is unsolved — "Waiting on a device event that has not been recorded yet is a no-op, so a consumer could sail past a layer the loader thread has not submitted."

quote: Long-context prefill is a major bottleneck for LLM inference: 1. **Quadratic attention complexity**: Full attention is O(N^2) in sequence length, making 256K+ contexts extremely slow 2. **Memory bandwidth** : Large KV caches stress memory subsystem — Tensor Parallelism (TP) helps by distributing model weights, but each GPU still processes the full sequence. title: Should the scheduler order the waiting queue by cache affinity (the ordering half of prefix-cache payoff)?
who: fululi12 / vLLM project — open PR #54625 "[Core][V1] Add cache-aware admission ordering"
quote: Within a bounded look-ahead window over the waiting queue, admit requests whose prefix is already resident in the KV cache ahead of requests that would have to compute theirs. The problem is an interaction between strict FCFS admission and prefix caching: a cold request admitted first allocates blocks, and under pressure that allocation evicts blocks which a request further back in the queue still needs. The eviction turns a would-be cache hit into recomputation, and the deeper the shared prefix, the more expensive the loss.
missing: The feature is not merged and both flags are off by default — "Two new scheduler options, both off by default: --cache-aware-admission-window N, default 0 ... --cache-aware-admission-threshold F, default 0.0". Scope is also explicitly restricted: "It requires the fcfs policy. Positional reordering is meaningless in a priority heap".

title: How should hybrid Mamba/GDN cached state be thinned under LRU pressure?
who: alphabetc1 / SGLang — Draft PR #38000 "[Mamba] Thin cached states by coverage instead of evicting the LRU tail"

missing: The PR motivation gives the precise failure mode for a **branching shared prefix on a single GPU**: "On a hybrid Mamba/GDN model every chunked-prefill boundary donates one Mamba state into the radix tree, so a long prompt pushes len / chunked_prefill_size states through the Mamba LRU. The LRU evicts a path's states shallow-first (they were inserted first), which is the inverse of what a branch match needs: a request that shares a 40k prefix and diverges mid-way is gated on the Mamba state at the divergence point, and the shallow states are exactly the ones that are gone. title: Prefix-cache retention is one global scalar; hit-inert EAGLE sliding-window draft groups still spend the shared LRU
who: vLLM contributor RFC #54661
quote: On hybrid models that carry an EAGLE-style sliding-window draft group (DFlash/DSpark-shaped drafters), that group hashes `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) + 1` block ids at *every* prefix-cache boundary and frees them *cached* onto the protected tail of the one LRU that all groups share, while — once it is exempted from the hit `min` — contributing nothing to the reconciled hit length. title: Cache-aware admission ordering inside the engine (FCFS admission destroys pending cache hits)
who: vLLM PR #54625 by fululi12, open
quote: Within a bounded look-ahead window over the waiting queue, admit requests whose prefix is already resident in the KV cache ahead of requests that would have to compute theirs. The problem is an interaction between strict FCFS admission and prefix caching: a cold request admitted first allocates blocks, and under pressure that allocation evicts blocks which a request further back in the queue still needs. The eviction turns a would-be cache hit into recomputation, and the deeper the shared prefix, the more expensive the loss. New flags are declared off by default: "Two new scheduler options, both off by default: Flag Default Meaning --cache-aware-admission-window N 0 Look-ahead depth over the waiting queue; 0 admits strictly in arrival order".
missing: A merge decision, and any published measurement. This is the same mechanism that was dropped in ABANDONED-1 ("A `CacheAffinityScheduler` plugin loadable via `--scheduler-cls` that reorders the V1 waiting queue by cached-prefix length before each scheduling iteration."), whose post-mortem measured +0.2%, so the open question is whether the new formulation clears the bar the old one missed. The sibling open PR #54366 "[Core] Add waiting-queue-informed KV cache eviction" addresses the eviction half.

title: vLLM's GPU-side `BlockPool` has no policy knob at all — only a single LRU/FIFO free queue
who: `sjmshsh` (author) in vLLM; issue state is `OPEN` with `"stateReason":"REOPENED"`, label `feature request`, created 2026-04-19, last updated 2026-08-21.
quote: vLLM's GPU KV cache (`BlockPool`) uses a **single-queue LRU** implemented in`FreeKVCacheBlockQueue`. When a request finishes, its blocks are appended to the tail of the free queue. When new blocks are needed, eviction drains from the head. This design has one fundamental blind spot: **once `ref_cnt` drops to zero, all blocks are equal candidates for eviction, regardless of how many times they were previously reused.** A system-prompt block touched by 10,000 requests and a one-time-use block are indistinguishable at eviction time.
missing: no `gpu_eviction_policy` flag exists. Confirmed against the local vLLM tree: `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py` still holds exactly one `self.free_block_queue = FreeKVCacheBlockQueue(self.blocks)` and no policy registry; the pluggable `CachePolicyFactory` exists only under `vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/policies/` (offload tier), not for HBM blocks.

title: Eviction across replicated KV tiers has no principled policy (published open problem)
who: the authors of "From Tensor Buffer to Distributed Memory Hierarchy: A Survey of KV Cache Management for LLM Serving" (arXiv 2607.02574), §6 design-gap agenda.
quote: DG3—Eviction across replicated tiers. A KV block can be live in HBM, host DRAM, and a remote store simultaneously. Existing tier-aware systems often approximate this with per-tier heuristics. A principled policy would price each tier's fetch latency against the probability of near-future reuse, which requires per-block reuse-distance and lifetime traces. MG4 and MG5 are therefore prerequisites.

title: SGLang's FP8 KV-cache decode path is unfused and slower than BF16 at small batch / short context

On memory-bound decode with small batches, this overhead outweighs the 2× reduction in KV read traffic." The reporter quantifies it: "For a model with ~64 layers, this is 64+ × 3 = ~192 .to() launches per forward pass. Each .to() has ~2-5μs launch overhead → ~400-1000μs of pure launch overhead per decode step, comparable to the entire attention computation on small batches."

title: RFC — back-pressure detection for KV cache offloading tiers
who: bnellnm, vLLM RFC issue #50031
quote: vLLM's KV cache offloading framework (CPU DRAM, local NVMe, shared storage) does not detect or respond to bandwidth saturation on secondary tiers. When a tier is saturated — whether from concurrent eviction, excessive store operations, or high IOPS — the system continues dispatching load/store jobs that pile up, further degrading bandwidth for actual serving loads. and "**Saturated-Tier bottleneck: In the case when multiple secondary tiers are specified, all tiers receive the same amount of stores. The CPU blocks are protected from eviction, when the stores are in progress and are released only when the slowest tier has completed the store. Here the slowest tier becomes the bottleneck for the entire system. Further, we observe CPU tier running out of memory, preventing further offloads."
missing: The RFC states its own scope limit verbatim: "The initial implementation adds back-pressure detection to secondary offloading tiers and a single response policy: drop store (write) requests to a tier that is under pressure. No load prioritization, tier rerouting, or load-vs-recompute decision is included in this phase." So load prioritization, tier rerouting, and any load-vs-recompute decision remain unsolved.

title: Unread tiered promotions are evicted by other speculative promotions (open PR, unfixed)
who: AlejandroParedesLT, vLLM PR #50014 (open, fixes #49902)
quote: TieringOffloadingManager promotes secondary-tier blocks to the primary CPU tier on every lookup() , including probes for waiting requests the scheduler ends up skipping that step (a request that defers is continue d past, not break ed on, so one schedule() pass can walk the whole waiting queue and issue a promotion per secondary-tier hit). Under many concurrent, disjoint-working-set requests, one promotion's landed-but-not-yet-GPU-read block could be evicted by another promotion before ever being consumed ... The evicted data gets re-promoted (and re-evicted) on a later step, burning secondary-tier I/O on data that never gets used.
missing: The fix (track landed-but-unread promotions and protect them) is proposed but the PR is still open — the shipping tiering manager has no protection for in-flight promotions.

The request therefore recomputes the full prefix even though the data is present in L3.
